young.html: R. H. Tawney was an English teacher and historian. He taught working men and women in evening classes, fought as a soldier in the First World War, and afterward wrote a book asking: what is all our work and business for?

Think of a bakery. Its purpose is to make good bread for the town. The baker who gets up at four to bake is paid for doing that job. Tawney believed that money and property should go mainly with doing a useful job, which he called a function. He worried about a society where getting rich becomes the goal in itself, which he called an acquisitive society.
Many people disagreed with him, and the lesson gives their side too: they said that owning, saving and taking risks are useful jobs as well, and that free markets let people decide what is useful.

young.name: gb-tawney-sort
young.cap: Sort each income as Tawney would. Then read what his critics said.

young.html: What is it for? Pick three jobs you know (a nurse, a farmer, a store owner). For each, write what the job is for: what good it does for others. Is anyone paid without doing a job? Talk about whether that is fair, and why people disagree.

full.html: R. H. Tawney (1880–1962) was an economic historian at the London School of Economics and a devoted teacher in the Workers' Educational Association. A Christian and a socialist, he was badly wounded at the Battle of the Somme in 1916. The Acquisitive Society (1920), written as Britain argued about how to rebuild after the war, made his name. He later wrote Religion and the Rise of Capitalism (1926) and Equality (1931).

Tawney's central idea is function: an activity that serves a social purpose. In a healthy society, he argues, rights, including property rights, are tied to functions: you hold them because of the service you perform. In what he calls an acquisitive society, rights stand on their own, and getting wealth becomes the main aim. He describes its appeal fairly, and then its danger:

full.text: It is an invitation to men to use the powers with which they have been endowed by nature or society, by skill or energy or relentless egotism or mere good fortune, without inquiring whether there is any principle by which their exercise should be limited.
full.author: R. H. Tawney
full.work: The Acquisitive Society, Chapter III (The Acquisitive Society)
full.ed: Harcourt, Brace and Howe, New York

full.html: Tawney does not attack all property. A farmer's land, a craftsman's tools and a family's home are bound up with work and life. What he criticizes is "passive" property that pays its owner without any service, his example being royalties paid to landowners on coal they neither found nor mined.

full.text: For it is not private ownership, but private ownership divorced from work, which is corrupting to the principle of industry.
full.author: R. H. Tawney
full.work: The Acquisitive Society, Chapter VI (The Functional Society)
full.ed: Harcourt, Brace and Howe, New York

full.cap: Tawney's distinction, with the replies of his critics.

full.text: If, as is patent, the purpose of industry is to provide the material foundation of a good social life, then any measure which makes that provision more effective, so long as it does not conflict with some still more important purpose, is wise, and any institution which thwarts or encumbers it is foolish.
full.author: R. H. Tawney
full.work: The Acquisitive Society, Chapter VI (The Functional Society)
full.ed: Harcourt, Brace and Howe, New York

full.html: His proposals (our summary): treat industry more like a profession, such as medicine, with standards of service; give those who do the work, including managers and engineers, a real voice in running it; and end payments for ownership that performs no function. He expected different forms of ownership in different industries, public in some and private in others.

Tawney's book was widely read, especially in Britain's labor movement and among Christian social thinkers. Its critics raised strong objections. Economists of the free-market school, such as Ludwig von Mises and Friedrich Hayek, argued that no authority can know which activities serve society best; prices and profits, set by people's free choices, are how a society finds out. They added that income from property is not "passive": it rewards saving, risk and the work of putting capital where it is most useful, and that private property spread widely protects personal freedom against government power. Others asked who would decide what counts as a "function," and warned that giving that power to officials could be worse than the problem. Defenders of Tawney reply that he wanted moral purpose, not central planning, and that his questions about the purpose of economic life are still worth asking.
Thinking Tawney wanted to abolish all private property. He defended property tied to work and use, and argued against ownership "divorced from work."

items: Aristotle's Politics distinguished household management from money-making for its own sake; Tawney revives that line.
Aquinas and medieval writers held that economic life is under moral law; Tawney admired that tradition and studied its decline.
Locke grounded property in labor; Tawney asks what happens when property no longer has any link to labor.
Adam Smith argued that self-interest in free markets, guided as if by an invisible hand, serves the common good; Tawney's critics stand nearer to Smith.
Veblen, the rung before this one, also criticized wealth cut off from useful work.
What is the purpose of work and business?
Is income from owning things fair? When?
Who should decide what is useful to society: buyers and sellers, or someone else?
Can a profession like medicine be a model for all work?

questions: What is the purpose of a job in your family or neighborhood? Who does it serve?
Is a person who saves money and lends it doing useful work? Why do people disagree?
Tawney thought some rights should depend on doing a service. Can you think of a right that should not?
Who decides what is useful: the people who buy things, or someone else?
Why might a soldier coming home from a terrible war ask what society is for?
